Listen to this article Share Unreliable electricity supply is forcing young Nigerians to find alternative ways to keep their businesses and livelihoods running, as the country’s persistent power deficit continues to raise operating costs and restrict economic opportunities. From digital creators and freelancers to tailors and small business owners, many are turning to solar energy to reduce their dependence on the national grid and expensive petrol and diesel generators. Read also: Taiwanese consortium targets multi-billion solar energy investment in Nigeria, seeks government support However, the cost of acquiring clean energy systems remains a barrier for many, particularly those operating small businesses with limited capital. The scale of the challenge remains significant. More than 85 million Nigerians lack access to grid electricity, making the country the largest contributor to the global electricity access deficit, according to the World Bank. Millions of others connected to the grid contend with irregular supply, with rural communities often facing longer periods without electricity. The consequences extend beyond household inconvenience. Poor electricity access limits the ability of small businesses to operate consistently, affects productivity in schools and healthcare facilities, and makes it harder for farmers to preserve and process agricultural produce. For young people seeking to build businesses and secure employment, unreliable power adds another layer of financial pressure. Read also: Solar energy is becoming an alternative to an unreliable grid electricity in Nigeria Against this backdrop, efforts to expand access to renewable energy are increasingly looking towards young people as contributors to solutions, rather than simply beneficiaries of energy interventions. The Network of Youth for Sustainable Initiative (NGYouthSDGs), in partnership with the Global Initiative for Food Security and Ecosystem Preservation (GIFSEP), has introduced a national youth competition to support community-led initiatives that promote solar energy access. The competition forms part of the second phase of the Solar Power Nigeria project, launched by GIFSEP in February 2026 to advocate for affordable and inclusive energy access, particularly for women, people with disabilities and economically vulnerable communities. Joshua Alade, executive director of NGYouthSDGs, said the electricity challenge was directly connected to the ability of young Nigerians to earn a living and participate in the economy. “Energy access and decent work are the same conversation, and we have been treating them as two,” Alade said. He noted that unreliable electricity makes it difficult for young entrepreneurs to sustain their businesses, arguing that access to dependable power should be considered essential infrastructure for employment and economic participation. “You cannot ask a young tailor, a digital creator, or a small business owner to build a livelihood when the power goes off for most of the working day,” he said. Read also: Why holiday shoppers are investing in solar energy The competition will invite Nigerians aged 18 to 35 to develop three-month campaigns or practical community projects aimed at improving solar energy access in specific states or communities. Entries opened on November 11 and will close on November 24, 2026. Seven successful applicants will receive grants of N390,000 each, alongside mentorship and opportunities to engage with energy sector partners and policymakers. Two outstanding participants will also nominate a public primary school or government health facility to receive a solar photovoltaic system, which the organisers will procure and install. Michael David, executive director of GIFSEP, said electricity access was also critical to addressing challenges in healthcare, agriculture and environmental protection. A health facility without reliable power, he said, cannot adequately preserve vaccines, while farmers without access to electricity face difficulties storing and processing their produce. Joseph Ibrahim, Nigeria campaign director of the Secure Energy Project, said women, people with disabilities and poor communities must remain central to efforts to address energy poverty. Read also: Taiwanese consortium targets multi-billion solar energy investment in Nigeria, seeks government support He said young Nigerians were already demonstrating the potential of clean energy in their homes and businesses, adding that supporting their ideas with funding could help extend those benefits to more communities. The broader challenge, however, goes beyond encouraging individual adoption of solar energy. Expanding access will also require affordable financing, reliable infrastructure and policies that make clean energy systems accessible to households and businesses that cannot afford the upfront cost of installation.
